rationale: Start with a broad gradient at moderate temperature to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window will guide subsequent gradient trimming.
Keep the gradient unchanged and test higher temperature to shift selectivity of the sole unresolved pair. This also shortens retention, preserving the time-term advantage.
Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Monitor the first pair, whose resolution of 1.67 provides only a modest margin.

Narrow the gradient window to recover first-pair resolution with a slope between those of injections 2 and 3. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction, supporting complete elution.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 4’s gradient slope to test whether the fully resolved separation can be accelerated. The first pair remains the key constraint; injection 4 is the established fully resolved fallback.

Trim the high-organic tail and shorten the gradient, keeping its slope only slightly steeper than the fully resolved injection 4. This should retain first-pair resolution near 1.5 while bringing the last peak out slightly earlier and still within the gradient.

Test a slightly steeper gradient to approach the first pair’s resolution limit while shortening the programmed ramp. The last peak may move into the final hold, so compare its retention time against injection 6 rather than assuming a shorter ramp means faster elution.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a steeper gradient to test whether a different elution-order regime allows a faster fully resolved separation. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 8 to test whether the late three-peak cluster separates while the early pair retains adequate resolution. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates temperature-driven selectivity changes.

Test an elevated starting organic fraction at 35 C to seek a faster alternative selectivity window. The temperature increase should spread the late cluster, while the changed starting fraction tests whether adequate early-pair separation can be retained.

At 30 C the early pair had favorable selectivity, but the late cluster needed a shallower gradient. Combine a shallower slope with a higher starting organic fraction to spread that cluster while offsetting the added retention time.

Test whether a substantially steeper gradient breaks the low-temperature three-peak coincidence through slope-dependent selectivity. This explores a faster separation regime while retaining low starting organic to protect the early pair.

Reduce the slope from injection 5 to recover early-pair resolution at the elevated starting fraction. This tests whether the time saved by starting stronger can compensate for the shallower gradient while maintaining maximum CRF.

Test a slope just steeper than injection 7 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary more precisely. The first pair may fall slightly below 1.5; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Make injection 10’s gradient shallower at unchanged starting composition and temperature to recover its sole unresolved pair. This tests a second fully resolved temperature regime, with the last peak expected to remain below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Test whether a stronger starting composition changes early-pair selectivity enough to enable a substantially faster separation at 35 C. This is exploratory: watch for early-peak compression and loss of resolution in the later cluster, retaining injection 7 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

With maximum CRF already achieved, test a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This offers a potentially more robust alternative to injection 7, whose critical pair is only just above 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 13 at the same starting composition and temperature, aiming to retain full resolution while shortening retention. This probes the resolution boundary for the higher-starting-organic alternative without risking incomplete elution.

Slightly steepen injection 17’s gradient to shorten retention and improve its limiting third–fourth pair, trading some excess first-pair resolution. This should preserve maximum CRF with more balanced resolution margins than the fastest boundary methods.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to compensate for early-pair compression. This probes whether another maximum-score method is available before attempting further shortening; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Steepen injection 19’s gradient one composition step to shorten retention while retaining a useful resolution margin. This should preserve maximum CRF; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Use a slope between injections 21 and 22 to shorten retention relative to injection 21 while retaining more first-pair resolution margin than injection 22. The final composition should keep the last peak within or near the end of the gradient, preserving maximum CRF.

Trim the gradient window at the higher starting fraction and use a slightly shallower slope than injection 13 to add first-pair resolution margin. This should retain maximum CRF with all peaks eluting below 10 minutes, while testing a shorter programmed gradient for that alternative.
